workIntro.lead: A bunch of projects from over the years. Some ended up on thousands of devices, some were failures, but all of them taught me something.

career.blurb: Where my development career started, as an intern at a digital 3D agency. After that they hired me as a VR developer, building immersive experiences and supporting them at conventions. I also assembled the office PCs myself.
career.detail: My developer career began at Letink Design, building VR and AR applications for the construction sector, tourism and government, publishing them online and supporting clients on location at trade fairs and events. On the side I made explainer animations, built interactive installations and assembled the office PCs myself.

career.blurb: A development studio where I worked across games and XR and grew from intern to team lead. It’s where I found out this was the right career for me.
career.detail: At DTT I started as an intern and grew into helping lead a team of developers across VR, Android, iOS and web projects. My responsibilities included selecting and mentoring new developers, improving the team's ways of working, and building features like deep linking, iOS plugins, XR, multiplayer, in-app purchases and optimisation.

career.blurb: For Zwijsen I designed, built and shipped AR seek-and-find and audiobook apps for children’s books, on my own from start to finish. It taught me that the last 10% (support, store reviews, weird feedback) is most of the work.
career.detail: As a freelancer for publisher Zwijsen I built AR seek-and-find and audiobook apps for children's books. Doing everything from designing, developing, testing and publishing on store pages. The apps were opened through QR codes in the books and gathered tens of thousands of downloads with exclusively positive reviews.

career.blurb: Casual mobile games for very large audiences. They’re on millions of devices and have to stay fun AND stable for a long time. Popcore is where I grew fastest as a developer.
career.detail: Looking for a new challenge I joined Popcore to build hyper-casual games for a huge Android and iOS audience. I ran live-ops on titles like Parking Jam, Pull the Pin and Wrecking Ball, and implemented new game modes, multiplayer features and tools for editors and level designers, everything on an ECS framework for speed and flexibility. Popcore is where I grew fastest as a developer.

career.blurb: Wonderment does location-based XR, anchoring digital experiences to real places to tell stories about them. I’m proudest of a tour I came up with about the Market Garden landings at my birthplace, a story I really wanted to help tell.
career.detail: I joined Wonderment to follow my enthusiasm for AR, building location-based experiences: visualisations, games and web applications, plus R&D into image recognition with machine learning in Unity and Lens Studio. My biggest focus was VPS and Cesium, technology that pins AR to the outside world with centimetre accuracy, to enrich environments with geodata like GIS, 3D map tiles and geoJSON.

career.blurb: The IT consultancy my recent assignments run through. Philips, Alliander and the Marechaussee all came through Rebels, so I’ve been moving between health care, energy and defence, each with its own rules.
career.detail: Rebels is the agency my recent assignments run through. Philips' immersive lab, Alliander and the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee are all placements under it, which has meant moving between health care, energy and defence. Different domains with different security constraints, all worth learning from the inside.

career.blurb: Medical XR and AI prototyping at the immersive lab, pushing new spatial tech toward something dependable enough to actually be useful. A lot of research is finding out what isn’t worth building, and it’s better to find that out early than late.
career.detail: At Philips' immersive lab I visualised medical equipment like CT scanners and new procedures. I built VR experiences that are both educational and informative used to familiarise people with new medical developments and to present them at trade fairs.

career.blurb: For Alliander I worked on bringing XR into their operations. In a small team we built a HoloLens prototype for placing transformer stations on the real street. If it were up to me, it would have run on an iPad.
career.detail: For Alliander I worked in a small dedicated team to build HoloLens software that lets field crews enrich their surroundings with information from the grid database, making the construction of voltage stations more efficient. I was responsible for the development, optimisation and UX of these apps.

career.blurb: Back at the immersive lab, this time in Unreal, building digital humans whose faces change colour with their heartbeat. We used them to train AI to read a pulse from video, for a wider range of skin types.
career.detail: At Philips immersive lab we started a project where we dived into research papers and built the first Unreal metahumans that realistically mimic a person's heartbeat in face coloration. This we use to generate synthetic data to train LLMs in detecting heartbeat from a distance more accurately and for more varied skin types.

career.blurb: At the Dutch military police I connect VR players inside a training simulation that’s been in development for years, with all the security that comes with it.
career.detail: For the Dutch military police I work on connecting VR players inside a complex training system that has been in development for years, given the security I had to build a lot of networking components myself and learn how they work in detail.

about.title: making computers do unusual things since 2016
about.lead: I’m a creative technologist from Utrecht. For almost a decade I’ve been chasing the same little moment, when a piece of technology stops feeling like technology and starts feeling like *a small magic trick*. I’m not bored of it yet.
body: Most of my work happens somewhere between the screen and the real world. I’ve put virtual objects in public spaces, turned children’s books into AR seek-and-find games and had strangers racing tiny AR cars across the same table. I like being close to the machine, down in the pixels, the code and the hardware, but I care just as much about the people holding it and *what happens when it all has to connect*.

A lot of what I know came from *breaking things*, sometimes on purpose. I like getting my hands on technology early, while the documentation is half written and nobody is sure yet what it can do. For my graduation I built a framework to get ARKit and ARCore working together, back when they were two separate worlds. Everyone is pretending until they figure it out, me included, and the unfinished parts are usually where the interesting questions are.

I have a theory I keep coming back to: *the demo lies to you*. A prototype on my desk can look like the future, but the real world always gets the final word. Networks disappear, hardware does strange things and someone will always use my carefully designed interface in a way I never imagined. At one trade show a brand-new server SDK kicked players out after about ten minutes. There was no fix in sight, so the game started telling them they’d won and should pass the phone to the next visitor.

Right now I’m connecting VR players for the Dutch military police, as a consultant through Rebels. Security is tight there, so I ended up building a lot of the networking myself, which turned out to be a good way to really learn how it works. On the side I’m experimenting with projection mapping for art installations, like one where people drew butterflies on paper and then watched them fly off into the trees. And I try to keep up with AI frameworks, which is a job in itself. If you like thinking about what technology can do, *we’ll probably have something to talk about*!
